nameStory: This harvestman's scientific name 'bracchiolum' comes from the Latin word for 'little arm,' likely referring to its distinctive leg proportions or arm-like appendages. Like all harvestmen, it's often called a 'daddy longlegs,' though this name creates confusion since it's shared with cellar spiders and crane flies that look quite different.
description: This is a harvestman (also called daddy longlegs), which looks like a spider but is actually a different type of arachnid altogether. It has a compact, oval body that appears as one unit rather than the distinct head-and-abdomen of true spiders. Its most striking feature is its extremely long, thin legs that can span several inches, making it appear much larger than its small body would suggest. The body itself is typically small, usually less than half an inch long.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The body appears as a single oval unit, not divided into two segments like a spider - run your finger gently over it and you'll feel it's all one smooth piece

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Eight extremely long, thin legs that feel delicate and wire-like to the touch, often several times longer than the body itself

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two small eyes positioned on a small bump or turret on top of the body, giving it a periscope-like appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in a characteristic bouncing gait and will often 'freeze' when disturbed, holding perfectly still with legs extended

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body is quite small and compact, typically less than half an inch long, but leg span can reach 2-3 inches across

habitat: Found in various habitats throughout New England, from woodlands to gardens and parks. They prefer areas with some moisture and vegetation cover, often hiding under logs, in leaf litter, or among low-growing plants during the day. You might spot them on tree trunks, garden walls, or even the sides of buildings in the evening.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and becoming active as temperatures warm. Look for them starting to appear under logs and in garden areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered. They're often seen at dusk and into the evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek overwintering sites. Mating occurs during this season in many harvestman species.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs that will hatch the following spring.

funFact: Unlike spiders, harvestmen can actually detach their own legs on purpose as an escape mechanism - the detached leg will continue twitching for several minutes to distract predators while the harvestman escapes, though the leg never grows back!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cellar spiders (another type of 'daddy longlegs'), but harvestmen have bodies that look like one piece rather than two distinct segments, and they don't make webs. Remember: if it has a web, it's a spider; if the body looks like one oval piece, it's a harvestman.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'daddy longlegs' is confusingly applied to three completely different creatures: harvestmen (like this one), cellar spiders, and crane flies (which aren't even arachnids). This leads to widespread mix-ups in identification and mythology about their supposed toxicity.
compareHints: Distinguishing this species from other Leiobunum harvestmen requires close examination of details like leg proportions and body markings that aren't easily visible in the field. The Eastern Harvestman (Leiobunum vittatum) is much more common and has a distinctive dark stripe down its back, while the Golden Harvestman has a noticeably yellowish coloration. Most field identification of harvestmen stops at the family level unless you're examining specimens closely.
